transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I suppose what brings me in today is... well, it's my mind, really. It just won't stop. I’ve always been a very organized person, you know. I got my degree, I managed things perfectly well for decades before I stopped working, and I’ve always relied on being thoroughly prepared for any situation. 

But... what brings me in is that I just can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts. It’s like a faucet with a broken handle. I will literally sit there at the kitchen table and tell myself, out loud sometimes, that I’ve made the list, I’ve checked the dates on the calendar, and I’ve done absolutely everything I reasonably can to prepare for whatever it is. It could be something as simple as organizing a small family get-together or just handling the week's paperwork. But even knowing that, even looking right at my perfectly organized lists, the worry just keeps spinning and spinning. I'll just sit there going over it all again and again, and my husband will tell me to just let it go and relax since I'm supposed to be enjoying my retirement now, but I can't. I just cannot seem to shut the worry down, no matter how much logic I try to apply to the situation. It just takes on a life of its own.
Do you ever feel compelled to repeat certain actions or rituals, like checking things over and over?

Oh, no, no. I think I know what you mean, like having to turn the door lock three times or washing your hands until they are raw, the sort of things you hear about on television. No, it is nothing like that at all. I mean, yes, I make my lists, as I was just saying, and I do look at them, but it is not a ritual. I do not feel forced to physically go and check the stove or count the light switches or anything physical like that. 

It is more that I just sit there in my chair, maybe with my cup of tea—Earl Grey, usually, I have never been able to handle coffee in the afternoon, it makes me far too jittery—and my mind just runs through the list on its own. I will look at the paper, and I will see that I have checked off calling the caterer for my granddaughter's graduation party, and I know I did it. I do not need to call them again to check, I would never want to be a bother to them. But my brain will just start wondering if they wrote down the wrong date, or if they might bring the wrong food, or if I perhaps did not speak clearly enough on the phone when I placed the order. 

So I am not actually doing anything over and over, you see. I am just thinking it over and over. My husband, Richard, he always tells me that I have the paper right there and I should just put it away and enjoy my afternoon. And I do put it away, I really do. I can put the notebook in the drawer and walk away into the garden, but the thoughts just follow me out there. So, no, no physical rituals or anything like that. Just this endless mental loop that I cannot seem to break out of, even when I am just trying to mind my own business and prune the hydrangeas.
Is your worrying usually about a specific type of situation or topic, or does it cover a wide range of things?

Oh, it covers absolutely everything, I’m afraid. I really wish it were just one specific thing, because then perhaps I could just... well, find a solution and be done with it. But no, it's not like that at all. My mind just keeps roaming all over the place. It never just settles on one topic. 

Like, just the other morning, I was sitting down with my tea and my thoughts were jumping right to the exhibition schedule for the local arts council—I’ve helped organize their autumn showcase for a few years now, and usually it’s such a pleasant activity—but suddenly I'm fretting about whether the venue will double-book us. And then, before I can even process that thought or tell myself it's fine, my brain is already off worrying about my daughter's travel plans. She's flying out to the coast next week for work, and I start thinking about whether her layover is long enough, or what if there's a storm and she gets stranded in an unfamiliar airport late at night. 

And then, as if that isn't enough to be getting on with, I'll happen to glance out the kitchen window and start agonizing over whether the house gutters need fixing before the leaves really start falling. Richard said he’d look at them, but you know how it is, I worry about him being up on a ladder at his age, and then I worry about having to hire someone, and whether they'll do a good job. 

It's just a constant, exhausting stream of... well, everything. And the terribly frustrating part of it all is that these are just small things, really. Just everyday life things that normal people handle without a second thought. But when I get stuck in these loops, those small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much, much bigger. Like a delayed flight turns into a catastrophe, or a clogged gutter means the foundation of the house will flood and ruin everything we've worked for. It just cascades from one completely ordinary topic to the next, and I can't seem to rein it in.
Has this constant worrying affected your ability to enjoy or participate in activities you normally like to do?

Well, yes and no, I suppose. I mean, I haven't completely stopped doing the things I love, thank goodness. I still keep up with my garden, as I mentioned with the hydrangeas earlier, and I still go to my book club. We meet every second Tuesday, usually over at Margaret's house because she has that lovely enclosed sunroom, and for years I’ve always prided myself on being the one who not just reads the book, but really engages with it, looking up the author's background and taking little notes in the margins, you know? 

But lately... well, with my mind spinning so much about everything else, I find myself arriving at book club feeling quite scattered. I’m just arriving less prepared. Sometimes I haven't even finished the last few chapters because I spent the whole previous evening sitting in my chair, worrying about those gutters or my daughter's flight instead of reading. I’ll sit there with the book open in my lap, but I’m not really taking in the words at all. 

And it's the same with the local arts council. I told you about the autumn showcase... well, normally I would be the one coordinating the entire vendor list and the catering. I've done it for years, and I've always genuinely enjoyed the bustle of it, getting everything lined up perfectly. But this year, I actually had to call Susan—she's the council president, a very sweet woman but terribly disorganized, which is why I usually help—and I had to tell her I needed to step back. I turned down parts of the exhibition planning entirely, like the catering coordination. 

It just... it all feels so much harder to manage than it used to. I used to juggle all these things without a second thought. I'd have the garden pristine, the book read, the exhibition planned, all while I was still working full time! But now, even though I'm retired and should have all the time in the world, the worry just takes up so much space in my head that there isn't enough room left for the planning and the enjoyment. So I am still participating, yes, I haven't become a hermit or anything dramatic like that, but I'm definitely not doing things to the standard I used to, and it's terribly frustrating to feel like I have to say no to things I used to handle so effortlessly.
Has your worrying affected your relationship with your husband, Richard?

Oh, Richard? No, no, I wouldn't say it has affected our relationship in any real way. Not that I've noticed, anyway. I mean, we’ve been married for forty-two years this coming August, and you don't get through four decades together without learning how to weather a few little quirks, do you? 

He is a terribly patient man, my Richard. Sometimes I think he has the patience of an absolute saint, honestly. When I get into one of my... well, when my mind is just running a mile a minute and I'm fussing over the gutters or the arts council, he mostly just lets me talk it out. I know I mentioned earlier that he tells me to put my lists away and enjoy the afternoon, but he always says it in a very gentle way, you know? He's never snapping at me or getting frustrated. 

Just last night, actually, we were sitting in the living room—we always watch that British baking program on Tuesday evenings, it's such a wonderful comfort just watching people make cakes and biscuits—and I started going on and on about whether the car needed its oil changed before we drive up to see his sister next month. And he just patted my hand, paused the television, and said, "It's all taken care of, love." He just doesn't let it drive a wedge between us. 

So, no, we aren't arguing about it, and he hasn't been distant or anything awful like that. If anything, I just feel a bit guilty sometimes that he has to listen to me go on about these silly little everyday things. I start to fret that I'm boring him, or that he's secretly tired of hearing about it... well, there I go, I suppose I'm just worrying about the worrying now! But between us, as a couple? No, we're as solid as ever. We still have our morning tea together every single day, we still do the crossword puzzle at the kitchen table... it really hasn't changed us.
Have you experienced any physical symptoms like headaches, tremors, or fatigue as a result of your worrying?

Headaches or tremors? No, no, thank goodness, nothing like that. My hands are as steady as ever—I can still thread a needle on the first try, which is more than Richard can say these days! And I don't really get headaches, just the occasional dull ache if I've forgotten to drink enough water, but nothing I'd blame on the worrying. 

But the fatigue... oh, that is an entirely different story. The fatigue is really quite something lately, and it's terribly frustrating. It's the strangest thing, too, because you would think, being retired and not having to rush off to an office, I'd be wonderfully rested. And the silly thing is, I do sleep! I usually sleep right through the night without much trouble at all. 

But even when I sleep through the entire night, I wake up feeling... well, I wake up feeling as if I have already put in half a day. It's as if my brain was just spinning and spinning the whole time I was unconscious, doing all the worrying I couldn't do while I was awake. I'll get out of bed, and my body just feels so heavy. And it doesn't take much to completely wipe me out now. By the time I go out to the yard to water the garden beds—and I have those lovely raised beds which are supposed to be easier to manage, though they still need a proper soaking every morning—or even if I'm just sitting at the kitchen table trying to sort through the discussion papers for my book club, I find I just have to stop. I'll have to go find my chair in the sitting room, sit down, and just gather myself. 

I'll just sit there, looking out the window, feeling absolutely drained from doing almost nothing at all. It's just this deep, exhausting tiredness that never really seems to wash off, no matter how many hours I spend tucked in bed. It really does make you feel a bit useless, to be completely honest, needing to catch your breath after just watering some petunias and organizing a few sheets of paper!
Would you say that your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?

Distress? Well... I suppose it depends entirely on what you mean by distress, doesn't it? When I hear the word distress, I tend to picture something terribly dramatic, you know? Like someone pacing the floorboards in the middle of the night, tearing their hair out, or weeping into their handkerchief. And I'm certainly not doing anything like that! 

I remember when my younger sister, Claire, was going through her divorce back in the late nineties—now *that* was distress. She would call me at two in the morning, completely beside herself, going on and on about how she was going to manage the mortgage on that massive house they had just bought. It had this gorgeous wrap-around porch, truly beautiful, but the upkeep was just astronomical for one person, especially with the heating bills in the winter. She was in genuine distress, couldn't eat, couldn't think straight. 

But for me? No, I wouldn't use that word. It's not a crisis. It's more of a... well, it's like a constant, annoying hum in the background of my life. A nuisance, really. It makes me tired, as I just mentioned, and I get quite cross with myself for not being able to just switch it off. I'll be sitting there with a cup of Earl Grey—I actually switched to decaffeinated in the afternoons a few months ago, thinking maybe that would help quiet my mind, though I can't say I've noticed a tremendous difference, to be perfectly honest—and I just feel bogged down by all the fretting. 

I'm still functioning, of course. I'm still going about my day, making dinner, going to the garden center, but it just feels like I'm carrying around this heavy, invisible basket of chores and worries everywhere I go. So, no, I wouldn't say it's causing me a *lot* of distress, not in the grand scheme of things. It's just terribly, terribly bothersome.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain activities or situations because of your worrying?

Avoiding? Well, no, I wouldn't use the word avoiding. I certainly haven't just shut myself indoors and pulled the curtains, if that's what you mean! I still keep up with my regular things. I’m still out in the garden every morning, because goodness knows if you leave those raised beds for even a day or two in this weather, the tomatoes just give up entirely. And I'm still going to my book club on Thursday afternoons. 

But... well, I suppose I have been stepping back a bit. Just a little. For instance, with the book club, I’ve started arriving much less prepared than I ever used to be. I used to be the one who would read the book, tab the pages with those little colored sticky notes, and write down discussion points on index cards. I always liked to keep things moving if the conversation stalled, you know how it is when people just want to gossip instead of talking about the chapters. But lately, I just haven't had the bandwidth for it. I show up, and half the time I haven't even finished the reading, which is so wonderfully unlike me. Mary—she's the one who usually hosts—even asked if I wasn't enjoying the author, and I had to make up a silly excuse about being busy around the house. 

And then there's the arts council. We have our summer exhibition coming up soon, and usually, I'm the one who coordinates all the volunteers for the opening night reception. Making sure we have enough wine glasses, organizing the catering—which sounds simple, but you would be absolutely amazed at how complicated people can make a cheese platter! But this year... well, when the committee asked me to take it on again, I just looked at the planning schedule and I felt this wave of... I don't know. It just felt so much harder to manage than it used to. 

I just pictured myself lying awake at three in the morning, fretting over whether the napkins were the right shade of blue or if someone was going to forget the ice for the water pitchers. The worrying just takes up so much space in my head now that the actual planning feels impossible. So, I turned that part of it down. I told them I could only handle the front door ticketing this time. It felt awful to say no, it really did, because I’ve been doing it for years. So I am still involved, I'm not avoiding the exhibition entirely, it's just... I just can't seem to juggle all those pieces the way I used to. It's just become too much to manage.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy time with friends and family due to your worrying?

Enjoy time with them? Oh, no, no. I still very much enjoy my time with my friends and family. Thank goodness for that, right? If I couldn't enjoy my loved ones, well, what would be the point of it all? 

Take last Sunday, for example. My daughter, Emily—she lives just about forty minutes away, which is wonderful because we get to see her and the grandchildren quite often. Well, they came over for a late lunch. I made a lovely roast chicken with those little fingerling potatoes. I used rosemary from my own garden, actually, which always makes me feel so accomplished, even though rosemary is practically a weed once it takes root, you really can't kill it. But anyway, we sat around the dining table for hours. The kids were telling me all about their summer camp. Tommy is doing archery this year, which sounds incredibly dangerous to me, letting ten-year-olds shoot arrows, but Emily assures me they use very blunt tips and there's strict supervision. I did fret about it for a moment, just picturing him poking someone's eye out, but it certainly didn't ruin the afternoon! I was still laughing with them, listening to their stories, and just soaking it all in. 

And Richard and I still have our quiet evenings together. We play gin rummy on the back patio when the weather is nice. I still take great pleasure in beating him, which I do about seventy percent of the time, though he’ll claim it’s closer to fifty. So the enjoyment is absolutely still there. 

The worrying... well, it's like I said before, it's just this background noise. I might be sitting there enjoying my chicken and listening to Tommy talk about his camp, and part of my brain is just buzzing away about whether I left the sprinkler on too long or if I remembered to renew the car registration. But it doesn't rob me of the joy of being with my family. I wouldn't let it do that. I just... I just wish the buzzing would stop while I'm trying to enjoy them, if that makes sense. But the enjoyment itself? No, that hasn't gone anywhere at all.
Do you feel like your worrying is significantly interfering with your overall quality of life?

Significantly interfering? Overall quality of life... well, that’s quite a grand way to phrase it, isn't it? It sounds so sweeping. I suppose... well, as I was mentioning just a few minutes ago, it’s not as if my life has ground to a complete halt. I still very much keep up with the garden, because as any gardener will tell you, the weeds certainly don't care if you're feeling fretful! The bindweed this year has been absolutely relentless, just wrapping itself around the stems of my hydrangeas, so I simply have to be out there pulling it up every morning. And I’m still going to my book club, of course. 

But... yes, I suppose it is interfering, when I really stop and look at it, because of exactly what I was saying earlier. I’ve started arriving so much less prepared for things. Going to book club without having finished the chapters, or without my little index cards of discussion points—that used to be completely unheard of for me! I always took such pride in being the organized one, the one who kept the conversation on track. And then, you know, turning down those parts of the exhibition planning for the arts council... I really did have to step back from the main coordinating role this year, simply because the whole thing just feels so much harder to manage than it used to. 

It's like I just don't have the mental space for it anymore. With all this background worrying taking up room in my head, organizing the caterers and the volunteers just felt like climbing a mountain. So, I wouldn't say my life is ruined by any stretch of the imagination, but it does feel like it's... shrinking a little bit, perhaps? Or at least, my capacity to handle my usual responsibilities is shrinking. I'm still showing up to my life, but I'm just not able to juggle it all the way I used to, and that is terribly frustrating. It certainly takes the shine off my day-to-day routine, having to constantly compromise and step back from the things I used to excel at.
Would you say that your worrying is causing you more distress than you initially let on, perhaps affecting you more deeply than you've acknowledged?

More distress than I let on? Well... I don't know if I'd say I'm hiding anything, exactly. I mean, I'm sitting right here telling you all about it, aren't I? But... deeply affecting me... I suppose that's a fair question, given everything I've just been rambling on about. 

It's just that, well, I don't want to make a mountain out of a molehill. I'm 67 years old, I'm retired, I have a lovely home, a wonderful husband, beautiful grandchildren... I don't have any real problems, not in the grand scheme of things. There are people out there dealing with true tragedies, you know? So when I catch myself lying awake at night worrying about whether the caterers for the arts council are going to bring the right kind of crackers for the brie, I just feel so... silly. I feel silly even saying it out loud to you now. 

So I don't know if it's a deep distress, like some profound sorrow or anything like that. It's more of a... a persistent irritation. Like a pebble in your shoe that you just can't shake out. You can still walk, you can still get where you're going, but every step is just a little bit uncomfortable, and eventually, it wears a blister. And I suppose that blister is starting to sting a bit more than it used to. 

I mean, I look at Richard, and he can just sit on the patio with his newspaper and a cup of coffee, and he is entirely present in that moment. He's just reading the news and enjoying the morning air. And I look at him and I think, 'How do you do that? How is your mind just... quiet?' Because my mind is always running down a checklist of things that might go wrong, or things I might have forgotten, or things that haven't even happened yet but might happen next week. 

So, yes, maybe it is a bit more distressing than I like to admit, because it feels like a failure on my part. I should be able to just relax and enjoy my retirement. I've worked hard my whole life, I raised my daughter, I kept a nice home, and now I'm supposed to be in my golden years, enjoying the fruits of my labor, as they say. But instead, I'm fretting over bindweed and book clubs and ice pitchers. It's frustrating. It's very frustrating. But I don't know if I'd call it a deep, dark distress. Just a... a very persistent, very annoying buzzing that I can't seem to swat away.
Do you ever feel anxious when you're not actively worrying about something?

Anxious when I'm not actively worrying? That’s a very interesting distinction you’re making there. Let me really think about that for a moment... 

I suppose... no. No, I don't think I do. Because, you see, the feeling of being anxious is always tied to one of those specific thoughts I mentioned. It’s never just a physical feeling out of the blue, like a stomachache that comes on for absolutely no reason. If I'm feeling tense, it's because my brain is actively chewing on a problem. 

Like last night, for instance. Richard and I were watching one of those lovely British detective shows on PBS—*Midsomer Murders*, I think it was, though honestly, I lose track of all the quaint little English villages with unusually high crime rates. We were sitting on the sofa, I had my cup of chamomile tea, which I always have around eight o'clock to help settle me for the evening. And for a good twenty minutes, I was completely absorbed in the plot. Who poisoned the vicar, that sort of thing. I wasn't worrying about anything, and I wasn't feeling anxious at all. I was perfectly relaxed, enjoying the tea, enjoying the television program. 

But then, during a break—well, they don't really have commercials on PBS, do they? During that little intermission where they talk about upcoming shows, my mind just wandered. And suddenly I remembered that the property tax bill is due next week, and I couldn't remember if Richard had actually put the check in the mail or just left it on the entryway table. *That's* when the anxious feeling started. The tightness, the buzzing in my head. It started because the thought arrived first. 

So, if I don't have a specific worry running through my head—like the taxes, or Emily driving home in the rain, or the bindweed in the garden—no, I don't just sit there feeling anxious for no earthly reason. The physical anxiety and the mental worry, they're like... well, they're like a horse and carriage for me. The worry is the horse pulling the whole thing along. If there's no horse, the carriage just sits there perfectly still. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious without a specific worry attached to it. It always has a subject, even if the subject is something terribly mundane.
Do you find that your worrying is causing you to double-check or verify things multiple times during your daily activities?

Double-checking things? Well, let me think about that... I suppose it depends on what you mean by multiple times. I mean, anyone with a lick of sense checks to make sure the front door is locked before they go to bed, don't they? It's just common sense. 

But... well, I don't find myself doing it over and over again, like some sort of ritual, if that's what you're asking. I don't stand at the stove and check the dials five times before I can leave the kitchen. Once I check something, I generally trust that it's done. 

Like with the property taxes I mentioned earlier. Once I asked Richard about the check, and he assured me he'd dropped it in the post box on his way to the hardware store—he was picking up some new hinges for the garden gate, the old ones were rusting terribly—well, that was that. I didn't make him go back and check the box, and I didn't call the tax office to see if it arrived. I just took his word for it and crossed it off my mental list. 

Now, I might *worry* about it again later, mind you. I might think, "Oh, what if the post office loses it?" But that's just the worry spinning its wheels again. It doesn't actually make me go and perform a physical check. It's all up here in my head. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm constantly verifying things. I just fret about them instead! It's much less exhausting physically, I suppose, but terribly tiring mentally.
Do you feel that your worrying is impairing your ability to function in your daily life?

Impairing my ability to function? Oh, well, that sounds so terribly dramatic, doesn't it? Like I'm bedridden with the curtains drawn or something. I certainly wouldn't go that far. 

I mean, I still get up every morning at half-past six. I still keep up with the garden, though heaven knows that bindweed I mentioned earlier is practically a full-time job in itself. If you turn your back on it for two days, it’s strangling the hydrangeas. And I still go to my book club on Thursdays. We've been meeting for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We're reading one of those historical fiction novels set in World War II—everyone seems to be writing those nowadays, don't they? 

But... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, which I suppose is the whole point of me sitting in this chair... I have noticed a bit of a shift. I used to be the one who brought the discussion questions for the book club, all typed up, and I’d have all my notes ready with little sticky flags on the pages. Lately, I just... I find myself arriving much less prepared. I haven't even finished the last two chapters of this month's book because my mind is just too busy buzzing with all those other worries to actually focus on the page. I end up reading the same paragraph three times and still not knowing what happened to the main character.

And then there's the arts council. I mentioned the caterers for the exhibition earlier. Usually, I'd be managing the whole reception—the invitations, the floral arrangements, coordinating with the gallery director, making sure the ice pitchers are filled. I've done it for years. But this time around... I actually had to call Susan—she's the co-chair—and tell her I couldn't handle the floral committee or the guest list. I just turned those parts down entirely and handed them over to her. 

It just feels... harder to manage than it used to. The thought of juggling all those moving pieces, making sure the florist delivers on time and the RSVPs are tallied... it just made me feel so exhausted before I even picked up the telephone. 

So, am I functioning? Yes, of course I am. I'm still doing things. But I'm not doing them the way I used to, and I'm certainly not taking on as much, because it just takes so much more mental energy to get through it all with this constant background fretting. It's terribly frustrating to admit that at my age, but yes, I suppose it is getting in the way. Just a bit.
Do you find that your worrying is focused on a specific set of concerns or themes, or is it more free-floating and unpredictable?

Specific themes? Oh, heavens, no. I wish it were just one thing, like... well, like just worrying about finances or just worrying about health. That would almost be manageable, wouldn't it? Just having one tidy little box to put all that fretful energy into. But no, it's quite the opposite. It’s terribly unpredictable, just jumping from one branch to another like a frantic squirrel. 

My mind just keeps roaming, you see. For instance, just yesterday morning, I was sitting with my coffee, trying to look over the exhibition schedule for the arts council—we have a lovely watercolorist coming in from Portland, and getting her dates to line up with the gallery's availability is always such a headache. But before I even finished my first cup, my thoughts had completely drifted away from the watercolors and landed straight on Emily, my daughter. I started fretting over her travel plans. She has a conference coming up in Chicago, and the weather there can be so dreadful this time of year, and I just kept picturing her trying to navigate the airport shuttles in a sleet storm. 

And then, just because I was thinking about storms, I suddenly remembered the house. I looked out the kitchen window and started agonizing over whether the house gutters need fixing. Richard was supposed to clean them out in the autumn, but you know how these weekend projects get delayed, and I had noticed a bit of an overflow near the rhododendrons during the last heavy downpour we had. 

So it just roams constantly—from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to the gutters—with no real rhyme or reason to it. It's exhausting just trying to keep up with my own train of thought. And the worst part is... well, it’s that these are all perfectly ordinary, mundane things, aren't they? People deal with gutters and flights and schedules every single day without batting an eye. But when my mind gets hold of them, these small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much, much bigger. A clogged gutter isn't just a weekend chore; in my head, it becomes water seeping into the foundation, cracking the basement walls, ruining the entire house... it just snowballs out of nowhere. So, no, I wouldn't say it's focused on one specific set of concerns at all. It's just about everything, really.
Would you say that your worrying is causing you significant distress, even if it's not dramatically impacting your daily life?

Significant distress? Oh, I don't know if I'd use a word quite as heavy as that. Distress sounds so... well, so theatrical, doesn't it? Like a heroine in a Victorian novel wringing her hands and swooning on a chaise lounge. I certainly wouldn't say I'm doing anything like that! 

When I think of significant distress, I think of the time Richard had his knee replaced. That was back in, oh, 2014, I believe—yes, because Emily had just moved into her first apartment in Chicago and couldn't come back to help me. Now *that* was distress. The surgeon was running two hours behind schedule, the hospital waiting room was freezing cold and smelled faintly of bleach and boiled cabbage, and I was absolutely beside myself. I was pacing back and forth, convinced he was going to have a terrible reaction to the anesthesia, or that they'd operate on the wrong leg—you hear about those things on the news, don't you? I must have drank six cups of terrible hospital coffee just to keep my hands busy. That's what distress feels like to me. A real, sharp, agonizing panic. 

But this worrying I’ve been telling you about? It’s not like that at all. It’s not a sharp pain or a terrible crisis. It’s more like... well, it’s like a mosquito buzzing right by your ear when you’re trying to enjoy a quiet evening on the patio. You swat at it, and it goes away for a second, but then it’s right back, buzzing away, ruining your concentration. It’s an annoyance. A persistent, tiring annoyance. 

It wears me out, having to constantly bat away these thoughts about the gutters or the arts council, but I wouldn't say it leaves me distressed. I don't sit and cry about it. I just sit there with my tea and feel thoroughly irritated with my own brain for not letting me have a moment's peace. I suppose if I were truly in significant distress, I wouldn't be able to carry on with my book club or my gardening at all. So, no, I wouldn't use that phrase. It's just a very loud, very persistent buzzing that I'd dearly love to be rid of so I could just read a book in peace!
Are you having trouble sleeping due to your worrying?

Trouble sleeping? Oh, no, thankfully not. You would think so, wouldn't you? With all that... that frantic squirrel energy I was telling you about just a moment ago. You’d think I’d be lying there staring at the ceiling fan all night, tossing and turning. But actually, my sleep is quite good. 

Richard and I have always been very particular about our evening routine. By about half-past nine, the television goes off—we used to watch the late news, but honestly, with the state of the world these days, it's just too much gloom before bed, isn't it? So we turn it off, and I go up and read. Well, I try to read, even if I have to go over the same page a few times like I said. 

And I have one of those lovely memory foam pillows now. Anxious when I'm not actively worrying? That’s a very interesting distinction you’re making there. Let me really think about that for a moment... 

I suppose... no. No, I don't think I do. Because, you see, the feeling of being anxious is always tied to one of those specific thoughts I mentioned. It’s never just a physical feeling out of the blue, like a stomachache that comes on for absolutely no reason. If I'm feeling tense, it's because my brain is actively chewing on a problem. 

Like last night, for instance. Richard and I were watching one of those lovely British detective shows on PBS—*Midsomer Murders*, I think it was, though honestly, I lose track of all the quaint little English villages with unusually high crime rates. We were sitting on the sofa, I had my cup of chamomile tea, which I always have around eight o'clock to help settle me for the evening. And for a good twenty minutes, I was completely absorbed in the plot. Who poisoned the vicar, that sort of thing. I wasn't worrying about anything, and I wasn't feeling anxious at all. I was perfectly relaxed, enjoying the tea, enjoying the television program. 

But then, during a break—well, they don't really have commercials on PBS, do they? During that little intermission where they talk about upcoming shows, my mind just wandered. And suddenly I remembered that the property tax bill is due next week, and I couldn't remember if Richard had actually put the check in the mail or just left it on the entryway table. *That's* when the anxious feeling started. The tightness, the buzzing in my head. It started because the thought arrived first. 

So, if I don't have a specific worry running through my head—like the taxes, or Emily driving home in the rain, or the bindweed in the garden—no, I don't just sit there feeling anxious for no earthly reason. The physical anxiety and the mental worry, they're like... well, they're like a horse and carriage for me. The worry is the horse pulling the whole thing along. If there's no horse, the carriage just sits there perfectly still. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious without a specific worry attached to it. It always has a subject, even if the subject is something terribly mundane.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's worrying is impacting daily life activities due to fear of making mistakes
doctor.question: Do you find that your worrying is causing you to double-check or verify things multiple times during your daily activities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about compulsive double-checking or verifying behaviors, which are not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Double-checking things? Well, let me think about that... I suppose it depends on what you mean by multiple times. I mean, anyone with a lick of sense checks to make sure the front door is locked before they go to bed, don't they? It's just common sense. 

But... well, I don't find myself doing it over and over again, like some sort of ritual, if that's what you're asking. I don't stand at the stove and check the dials five times before I can leave the kitchen. Once I check something, I generally trust that it's done. 

Like with the property taxes I mentioned earlier. Once I asked Richard about the check, and he assured me he'd dropped it in the post box on his way to the hardware store—he was picking up some new hinges for the garden gate, the old ones were rusting terribly—well, that was that. I didn't make him go back and check the box, and I didn't call the tax office to see if it arrived. I just took his word for it and crossed it off my mental list. 

Now, I might *worry* about it again later, mind you. I might think, "Oh, what if the post office loses it?" But that's just the worry spinning its wheels again. It doesn't actually make me go and perform a physical check. It's all up here in my head. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm constantly verifying things. I just fret about them instead! It's much less exhausting physically, I suppose, but terribly tiring mentally.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's worrying is impacting their daily life to the extent that it could be considered an impairment
doctor.question: Do you feel that your worrying is impairing your ability to function in your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with the garden and book club, but I’ve started arriving less prepared and turning down parts of the exhibition planning because it feels harder to manage than it used to.

patient.answer:
Impairing my ability to function? Oh, well, that sounds so terribly dramatic, doesn't it? Like I'm bedridden with the curtains drawn or something. I certainly wouldn't go that far. 

I mean, I still get up every morning at half-past six. I still keep up with the garden, though heaven knows that bindweed I mentioned earlier is practically a full-time job in itself. If you turn your back on it for two days, it’s strangling the hydrangeas. And I still go to my book club on Thursdays. We've been meeting for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We're reading one of those historical fiction novels set in World War II—everyone seems to be writing those nowadays, don't they? 

But... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, which I suppose is the whole point of me sitting in this chair... I have noticed a bit of a shift. I used to be the one who brought the discussion questions for the book club, all typed up, and I’d have all my notes ready with little sticky flags on the pages. Lately, I just... I find myself arriving much less prepared. I haven't even finished the last two chapters of this month's book because my mind is just too busy buzzing with all those other worries to actually focus on the page. I end up reading the same paragraph three times and still not knowing what happened to the main character.

And then there's the arts council. I mentioned the caterers for the exhibition earlier. Usually, I'd be managing the whole reception—the invitations, the floral arrangements, coordinating with the gallery director, making sure the ice pitchers are filled. I've done it for years. But this time around... I actually had to call Susan—she's the co-chair—and tell her I couldn't handle the floral committee or the guest list. I just turned those parts down entirely and handed them over to her. 

It just feels... harder to manage than it used to. The thought of juggling all those moving pieces, making sure the florist delivers on time and the RSVPs are tallied... it just made me feel so exhausted before I even picked up the telephone. 

So, am I functioning? Yes, of course I am. I'm still doing things. But I'm not doing them the way I used to, and I'm certainly not taking on as much, because it just takes so much more mental energy to get through it all with this constant background fretting. It's terribly frustrating to admit that at my age, but yes, I suppose it is getting in the way. Just a bit.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is impacting their daily life to the extent that it could be considered an obsessive-compulsive trait, or if it's more aligned with generalized anxiety
doctor.question: Do you find that your worrying is focused on a specific set of concerns or themes, or is it more free-floating and unpredictable?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the focus of my worrying, specifically whether it's limited to certain themes or spans across various unpredictable topics. This directly relates to the symptom of excessive worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
Specific themes? Oh, heavens, no. I wish it were just one thing, like... well, like just worrying about finances or just worrying about health. That would almost be manageable, wouldn't it? Just having one tidy little box to put all that fretful energy into. But no, it's quite the opposite. It’s terribly unpredictable, just jumping from one branch to another like a frantic squirrel. 

My mind just keeps roaming, you see. For instance, just yesterday morning, I was sitting with my coffee, trying to look over the exhibition schedule for the arts council—we have a lovely watercolorist coming in from Portland, and getting her dates to line up with the gallery's availability is always such a headache. But before I even finished my first cup, my thoughts had completely drifted away from the watercolors and landed straight on Emily, my daughter. I started fretting over her travel plans. She has a conference coming up in Chicago, and the weather there can be so dreadful this time of year, and I just kept picturing her trying to navigate the airport shuttles in a sleet storm. 

And then, just because I was thinking about storms, I suddenly remembered the house. I looked out the kitchen window and started agonizing over whether the house gutters need fixing. Richard was supposed to clean them out in the autumn, but you know how these weekend projects get delayed, and I had noticed a bit of an overflow near the rhododendrons during the last heavy downpour we had. 

So it just roams constantly—from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to the gutters—with no real rhyme or reason to it. It's exhausting just trying to keep up with my own train of thought. And the worst part is... well, it’s that these are all perfectly ordinary, mundane things, aren't they? People deal with gutters and flights and schedules every single day without batting an eye. But when my mind gets hold of them, these small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much, much bigger. A clogged gutter isn't just a weekend chore; in my head, it becomes water seeping into the foundation, cracking the basement walls, ruining the entire house... it just snowballs out of nowhere. So, no, I wouldn't say it's focused on one specific set of concerns at all. It's just about everything, really.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant distress
doctor.question: Would you say that your worrying is causing you significant distress, even if it's not dramatically impacting your daily life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about clinically significant distress. While this is part of the distress/impairment criterion, the symptom profile only contains an item for 'Functional Impairment' (which was addressed in a previous turn) and does not have a separate item for distress.

patient.answer:
Significant distress? Oh, I don't know if I'd use a word quite as heavy as that. Distress sounds so... well, so theatrical, doesn't it? Like a heroine in a Victorian novel wringing her hands and swooning on a chaise lounge. I certainly wouldn't say I'm doing anything like that! 

When I think of significant distress, I think of the time Richard had his knee replaced. That was back in, oh, 2014, I believe—yes, because Emily had just moved into her first apartment in Chicago and couldn't come back to help me. Now *that* was distress. The surgeon was running two hours behind schedule, the hospital waiting room was freezing cold and smelled faintly of bleach and boiled cabbage, and I was absolutely beside myself. I was pacing back and forth, convinced he was going to have a terrible reaction to the anesthesia, or that they'd operate on the wrong leg—you hear about those things on the news, don't you? I must have drank six cups of terrible hospital coffee just to keep my hands busy. That's what distress feels like to me. A real, sharp, agonizing panic. 

But this worrying I’ve been telling you about? It’s not like that at all. It’s not a sharp pain or a terrible crisis. It’s more like... well, it’s like a mosquito buzzing right by your ear when you’re trying to enjoy a quiet evening on the patio. You swat at it, and it goes away for a second, but then it’s right back, buzzing away, ruining your concentration. It’s an annoyance. A persistent, tiring annoyance. 

It wears me out, having to constantly bat away these thoughts about the gutters or the arts council, but I wouldn't say it leaves me distressed. I don't sit and cry about it. I just sit there with my tea and feel thoroughly irritated with my own brain for not letting me have a moment's peace. I suppose if I were truly in significant distress, I wouldn't be able to carry on with my book club or my gardening at all. So, no, I wouldn't use that phrase. It's just a very loud, very persistent buzzing that I'd dearly love to be rid of so I could just read a book in peace!

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is impacting their sleep quality
doctor.question: Are you having trouble sleeping due to your worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sleep disturbance or trouble sleeping, which is not covered in my symptom profile. My profile includes Fatigue (S029), but that describes waking up tired despite sleeping through the night, not trouble sleeping.

patient.answer:
Trouble sleeping? Oh, no, thankfully not. You would think so, wouldn't you? With all that... that frantic squirrel energy I was telling you about just a moment ago. You’d think I’d be lying there staring at the ceiling fan all night, tossing and turning. But actually, my sleep is quite good. 

Richard and I have always been very particular about our evening routine. By about half-past nine, the television goes off—we used to watch the late news, but honestly, with the state of the world these days, it's just too much gloom before bed, isn't it? So we turn it off, and I go up and read. Well, I try to read, even if I have to go over the same page a few times like I said. 

And I have one of those lovely memory foam pillows now. My sister Margaret recommended it to me last Christmas because she was having terrible neck trouble, and while I don't have neck trouble myself, I thought, well, why not be as comfortable as possible? It really does cradle your head beautifully. So once I finally put the book down and turn out the bedside lamp... I suppose I'm just so thoroughly exhausted from batting away all those buzzing thoughts all day long that my brain just finally gives up the ghost. 

I am usually out like a light. I sleep right through until half-past six every morning. Occasionally the neighbor's cat—this enormous ginger tomcat, I have no idea who he actually belongs to, but he’s always prowling around our hydrangeas—might make a racket near the rubbish bins, but even that barely rouses me. So no, sleep is the one thing I really can't complain about. It's just the waking hours that are the tiring part!

Difficult? Well... I wouldn't say I've completely dropped the ball, if that's what you mean. I'm certainly not sitting around in my dressing gown all day! I still keep up with the garden, of course. The hydrangeas won't prune themselves, and I simply must stay on top of the weeding before the bindweed takes over the back fence completely. And I still go to my book club. We meet every second Tuesday—Margaret usually hosts, and she always makes these wonderful little lemon tarts. 

But... I suppose, if I'm being perfectly honest with myself, things have slipped a bit. I’ve started arriving at book club much less prepared than I used to be. We're reading a rather thick historical novel right now, and last week I found myself just staring at the same page for twenty minutes, my mind completely consumed by whether the chest freezer in the garage was making a strange humming noise. I ended up having to skim the last fifty pages right before the meeting, and I felt quite foolish when I couldn't really contribute to the discussion about the protagonist's motives. I just had to sort of nod along and eat my tart.

And it's affecting my volunteer work, too. I mentioned the arts council and the exhibition planning earlier, didn't I? Well, normally, I would be the one organizing the entire itinerary for our visiting artists—the welcome dinner, the hotel, the gallery walk-through. I've done it for years and I usually pride myself on getting all the ducks in a row. But lately... it just feels so much harder to manage than it used to. The thought of juggling all those schedules while my brain is already buzzing with a dozen other mundane worries... it was just too overwhelming. 

So, I actually called Susan—she’s our council president, lovely woman but terribly disorganized, bless her—and I turned down the itinerary planning for the Portland watercolorist. I told her I could only manage the mailing list this time. Susan was a bit taken aback, I think, because it’s so unlike me to step back like that. But I just couldn't face it. So, yes, I am still fulfilling my responsibilities, by and large, but I'm definitely having to scale back and say no to things just to keep my head above water.

The simplest tasks? Oh, no, no. I think we might be crossing our wires a bit, Doctor, because as I was just saying a moment ago, I certainly haven't ground to a complete halt!
